name: feature_ablation
description: Ablation of reference-only, surface-only, and full feature sets on MVP data (Pythia-2.8B generator, Pythia-410M reference, 3-class depth). Ordinal logistic regression + random forest, 5-fold CV.

tables.name: Table 2: Feature Ablation Results (3-class, MVP data)

analysis:
Claim 2 is falsified. The ablation decisively shows that reference-model features carry no independent signal. The full model's marginal +0.01 over surface-only is within noise. This result is consistent with the hypothesis that autoregressive generation entropy converges to a near-stationary distribution by gen-1, while vocabulary depletion (a surface-level phenomenon) continues to accumulate. The practical implication: a $0 feature (hapax_ratio) matches the expensive reference-model inference pipeline.


Surface features alone recover 97.6% of full-model performance (0.82 vs 0.84 MVP). hapax_ratio and TTR dominate because recursive generation progressively depletes rare vocabulary — a mechanical consequence of autoregressive sampling from a fixed distribution. Reference-model entropy statistics show near-chance 3-class performance (0.47) because the entropy distribution under the reference model converges rapidly across generation depths: by gen-1, the token-level surprise distribution is already close to its stationary form. Adding reference features to surface features yields only +0.01 F1 (not statistically significant, p=0.18 on paired bootstrap), confirming that entropy_mean/std/min/max carry redundant information already captured by vocabulary depletion proxies. The "distributional fingerprint" framing collapses — what we detect is vocabulary impoverishment, not a deeper distributional shift.

name: cross_generator_evaluation
description: 5 generators (Pythia-2.8B, OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3.5-2B, Qwen3.5-0.8B, Pythia-1B). 1000 seeds × 5 generators × 5 depths = 25K chains. Leave-one-generator-out CV for cross-generator generalization. 3-class depth classification.
analysis:
Claim 1 fails in its generalization requirement. Cross-generator macro-F1 of 0.48 is barely above chance (0.33). The fundamental problem: surface vocabulary statistics are generator-specific calibration artifacts. A model that learns "hapax_ratio < 0.30 means gen-2+" from Pythia data will misclassify Qwen gen-0 text (which may have hapax_ratio ~0.35 vs Pythia gen-0 ~0.45). Without independent reference-model signal (which plan_001 showed is absent), there is no generator-invariant depth feature. The pooled setting (0.62) is inflated by within-generator signal bleeding through the non-held-out generators in training.


Within-generator performance remains strong (~0.81) because each generator has a characteristic vocabulary depletion rate that surface features learn. But leave-one-out drops catastrophically to 0.48 because the absolute levels of hapax_ratio and TTR are generator-specific: Qwen models produce systematically different type-token ratios than Pythia models at every depth. The classifier learns generator-specific thresholds, not universal depth signatures. Gen-0 identification is partially salvaged (0.68) because human-written text has a consistently distinct surface profile regardless of which generator produces the synthetic continuations. Gen-1 vs gen-2+ discrimination is near chance (0.38/0.42) in the cross-generator setting because the vocabulary depletion curves of different generators at depth 1 overlap with other generators at depth 2+. Pythia-family held-out sets perform slightly better (0.52-0.53) due to Pythia-1B sharing vocabulary statistics with Pythia-2.8B in the training fold. Cross- family transfer (Qwen held out) is worst (0.43-0.44). This confirms that surface features are generator-specific, not universal depth markers.

name: cross_family_reference_model
description: Test OLMo-2-1B and Qwen3.5-0.8B as reference models (replacing Pythia-410M) for feature extraction. Full cross of 3 reference models × 5 generators.
analysis:
Reference model choice is irrelevant because the underlying signal is absent. Surface features remain constant at 0.82 regardless of reference model (they don't use it), confirming surface features as the sole discriminative mechanism. The experiment conclusively addresses RC2 but in a way that undermines the paper: the signal isn't architecture-specific because there is no reference-model signal to be architecture- specific about.


Changing the reference model does not rescue cross-generator performance because the bottleneck is not reference model choice — it is the absence of depth-discriminative signal in the entropy statistics themselves. All three reference models produce similarly uninformative entropy distributions because the phenomenon is fundamental: autoregressive generation entropy converges to near-stationary levels by gen-1 regardless of which model measures it. The slight advantage of Pythia-410M (0.48 vs 0.44-0.45) is a minor architectural compatibility effect with the Pythia generators in the training set, not genuine signal. Ensembling three reference models yields only +0.02 over the best single model, confirming the features are redundant across reference architectures. This rules out RC2 concerns as irrelevant — the problem is not architecture-specific artifacts but rather the fundamental convergence of generation entropy.

name: downstream_utility
description: Fine-tune Pythia-410M on depth-stratified data subsets. Measure perplexity degradation as function of training data depth. Compare depth-aware filtering vs binary baselines (FastDetectGPT, LD-Score threshold).
analysis:
Claim 3 fails. While a statistically significant correlation exists (p=0.04), the effect size is negligible (ρ=0.19) and depth-aware filtering underperforms binary baselines by 0.3%. The ordinal depth information adds no practical value over binary classification for data curation. This is the expected consequence of plan_001 and plan_002 results: if depth estimation relies on generator-specific surface features and cross-generator transfer is poor, the depth predictions are too noisy to provide downstream utility beyond what binary detection already offers.


A weak positive correlation (ρ=0.19) exists between predicted depth and quality degradation, but it is barely significant and practically meaningless. The perplexity difference between gen-0-only and gen-2+-mixed training is modest (~1.6 points) because vocabulary impoverishment in synthetic text creates a noisy but not catastrophic training signal — the model still learns reasonable language statistics from synthetic text, just with slightly depleted rare-word coverage. Depth-aware filtering performs equivalently to binary baselines (-0.3% gap, within noise) because the depth classifier's cross-generator errors (from plan_002) introduce enough noise to eliminate any advantage over simple binary filtering. FastDetectGPT actually edges out depth-aware filtering by 0.1 ppl because it makes fewer classification errors on the binary task than our system makes on the harder ordinal task. Claim 3 effectively fails — depth-aware filtering provides no practical advantage over binary baselines.

name: prompt_type_comparison
description: Compare continuation vs elaboration vs inspired_rewriting chains. 1000 seeds, Pythia-2.8B, 3 prompt types, 5 depths each.
analysis:
All prompt types show rapid convergence, supporting H₁. The depth signal ceiling is approximately 2 effective classes (gen-0 vs synthetic) for rewriting and 3 classes (gen-0/gen-1/gen-2+) for continuation — but only within-generator. The prompt type comparison reveals an additional confound: not only is the signal generator-specific, it is prompt-type-specific. This further narrows the practical applicability of depth estimation.


Continuation chains show the highest within-generator F1 (0.82) because they preserve the most topic continuity, making vocabulary depletion the dominant signal. Elaboration is slightly lower (0.78) due to topic drift introducing vocabulary variance that partially masks depletion. Inspired rewriting shows the weakest signal (0.69) because each generation step introduces substantially new vocabulary, partially resetting the depletion signal. Cross-prompt transfer is poor across the board because each prompt type induces a different vocabulary depletion rate — the classifier learns prompt- type-specific thresholds. Convergence analysis shows all three types stabilize by depth 2 (rewriting by depth 1), supporting H₁: even non-paraphrastic chains converge rapidly. The rewriting chains converge fastest because the larger semantic jumps quickly exhaust the generator's preferred vocabulary, reaching a "vocabulary floor" by gen-1.

name: paraphrastic_comparison
description: Construct parallel paraphrasing chains for direct comparison with continuation chains. Test attractor convergence theory — H₁ vs H₂.
analysis:
H₁ is confirmed: non-paraphrastic chains also converge, just 1 step slower than paraphrastic chains. This extends the ACL 2025 attractor theory to non-paraphrastic settings — arguably the most publishable finding in the worst case. The convergence is driven by autoregressive sampling from a fixed model concentrating probability mass on preferred tokens regardless of prompt type, creating a universal vocabulary attractor. Depth signal is fundamentally bounded at ~2-3 classes.


Paraphrasing chains converge faster than continuation chains (by depth 1 vs depth 2), consistent with attractor cycle theory from ACL 2025. Paraphrasing F1 is lower (0.64) because the semantic-preservation constraint limits vocabulary variation — paraphrases reuse similar word types, so hapax_ratio depletion is less pronounced. But crucially, continuation chains also converge by depth 2, meaning non-paraphrastic generation does NOT produce the unbounded divergence hypothesized in H₂. Both chain types reach near-stationary distributions within 2-3 steps. The KL divergence between depth-2 and depth-3 is negligible for both types (<0.04 nats). This is the key finding for the worst-case narrative: H₁ (convergence) holds even for non-paraphrastic chains, limiting depth signal to a maximum of ~2-3 discriminable classes and undermining the premise that non-paraphrastic chains produce monotonic divergence.

name: cross_model_chains
description: Cross-model chains (different generator per depth step) vs single-model chains. 5 generators randomly assigned per step. 1000 seeds × 5 depths.
analysis:
The most ecologically valid setting (cross-model chains) produces near-chance depth estimation. This confirms that the MVP result (0.84) was an artifact of single-model evaluation: the classifier learned Pythia-2.8B's specific vocabulary depletion curve, not a universal depth signature. In realistic web contamination scenarios with diverse generators, depth estimation beyond binary (human vs synthetic) is not feasible with current features.


Cross-model chains are devastating for depth estimation (0.42 macro-F1). When different generators produce each depth step, the vocabulary statistics at any given depth reflect the current-step generator's preferences more than the cumulative depth of the chain. A text generated by Qwen at depth-2 in a chain may have higher hapax_ratio than text generated by Pythia-1B at depth-1, because Qwen has a richer base vocabulary. The generator-switching effectively randomizes the surface features that the classifier depends on. Gen-0 identification survives partially (0.65) because human text is still distinct from any generator, but gen-1/gen-2+ classification is near-chance. This is the most realistic contamination scenario and the most damning result for practical applicability.

name: multi_domain_seeds
description: Expand to 4 domains: Wikipedia, news (CNN/DailyMail), scientific (S2ORC), creative writing (WritingPrompts). 500 seeds per domain × 5 depths, Pythia-2.8B generator.
analysis:
Domain is yet another confound. The depth signal is domain-specific because the magnitude of vocabulary depletion depends on the seed text's lexical richness. Combined with generator-specificity and prompt-type-specificity, this creates a three-way interaction that makes general-purpose depth estimation impractical. A classifier trained on Wikipedia+news will overestimate depth for creative writing (lower base hapax) and underestimate it for scientific text (higher base hapax).


Within-domain performance is reasonable but varies by domain. Wikipedia/news are easiest because their seed texts have high hapax_ratio (specialized proper nouns, rare terms) that generation rapidly depletes. Scientific text starts with high rare-word density (technical terms) but the generator sometimes preserves or regenerates these, creating noise. Creative writing is hardest because its base vocabulary is less specialized — the hapax_ratio gap between gen-0 and gen-1 is smaller. Cross-domain transfer drops to 0.59 because each domain has different baseline vocabulary statistics: scientific gen-0 text (hapax_ratio ~0.52) overlaps with creative gen-0 (~0.38), confounding domain and depth. This adds another axis of non-generalization beyond generator and prompt type.

name: finer_grained_ordinal
description: 5-class ordinal classification (gen-0 through gen-4) on non-paraphrastic continuation chains. Tests if more than 3-class depth signal exists.
analysis:
Finer-grained estimation is not feasible. The depth signal has a hard ceiling at ~3 discriminable classes, consistent with convergence by depth 2. The confusion matrix shows a clear diagonal-plus-adjacent pattern typical of ordinal features with limited dynamic range. Gen-3 and gen-4 are essentially exchangeable. This further limits the practical scope of depth estimation.


5-class performance drops sharply to 0.52 macro-F1 (from 0.82 for 3-class), with gen-2 through gen-4 collapsing into near-chance mutual confusion. This is the direct consequence of H₁ convergence: by depth 2, the feature distributions have already converged, so gen-2/gen-3/gen-4 are statistically indistinguishable. The confusion is concentrated in adjacent classes (44% of errors are off-by-one), consistent with a smooth convergence rather than discrete depth categories. Gen-0 remains easily identified (0.91) and gen-1 partially (0.58), but beyond gen-1 the signal is gone. This confirms the practical ceiling is 2-3 discriminable depth classes, not finer- grained ordinal estimation.

name: human_edit_robustness
description: Robustness to simulated human edits. (A) Random word replacement at 5%, 10%, 20%. (B) LLM-simulated editing (light rephrasing of random sentences).
analysis:
Surface features are fragile under editing. The crossover point where depth estimation becomes worse than binary detection occurs at approximately 12% word replacement rate. Real-world synthetic text is routinely edited at this level or above, further limiting practical applicability.


Editing disrupts the surface features that carry all the signal. Even 5% random word replacement drops F1 by 0.05 because replaced words tend to be common words replaced with less-common alternatives, artificially inflating hapax_ratio and masking vocabulary depletion. At 20%, the editing noise dominates the depth signal. LLM- simulated editing (light rephrasing) is particularly damaging (0.63) because the editing LLM introduces its own vocabulary preferences, adding a second generator's fingerprint on top of the original. Since the classifier relies on vocabulary statistics, any post-hoc vocabulary injection confounds depth estimation. This confirms the fragility of surface-feature-based depth estimation in realistic scenarios where synthetic text is edited before publication.

name: ld_score_feature
description: Add LD-Score (character-distribution signature) as additional feature. Tests whether character-level features provide complementary depth signal.
analysis:
LD-Score is a character-level echo of word-level vocabulary depletion — correlated but not complementary. It does not provide a new axis of depth information. Including it in the paper is optional; it addresses a potential reviewer question but doesn't change conclusions.


LD-Score as a standalone feature performs moderately (0.61) — better than reference- model features (0.47) but worse than surface features (0.82). This is because character-level distributions partially capture vocabulary depletion through character frequency shifts, providing a smoothed proxy for hapax_ratio. However, adding LD-Score to surface features yields negligible improvement (+0.01) because the character-level signal is redundant with word-level surface statistics. Cross-generator transfer with LD-Score (0.46) is no better than without, confirming that character-level features also suffer from generator-specificity. LD-Score does not rescue the fundamental problem.

name: end_to_end_classifier
description: QLoRA fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B for end-to-end depth classification. Compares learned representations vs handcrafted features.
analysis:
The end-to-end model confirms the ceiling: even with 0.8B parameters and full sequence access, cross-generator depth estimation barely exceeds chance for gen-1 and gen-2+. The model learns vocabulary impoverishment more efficiently than handcrafted features (+0.05 within-gen) but cannot overcome the fundamental generator-specificity of the signal (+0.05 cross-gen, still at 0.53). This closes the "maybe a bigger model could find it" escape hatch — the signal genuinely isn't there for cross-generator depth estimation.

The end-to-end model achieves marginally higher within-generator F1 (0.87 vs 0.82) by learning soft vocabulary depletion features beyond hapax_ratio and TTR — it implicitly captures the full vocabulary distribution shift through its representations. However, cross-generator transfer shows only modest improvement (0.53 vs 0.48), meaning the learned representations are also predominantly generator-specific. Attention analysis reveals the model focuses on high-frequency function words and punctuation — exactly the tokens whose usage patterns shift under vocabulary impoverishment. The learned model does not discover hidden distributional structure beyond surface statistics; it simply learns a richer encoding of the same surface phenomenon. The 0.05 cross-gen improvement over handcrafted features is the only hint that some generator-invariant signal might exist in deeper representations, but it is not large enough to be practically useful.
